# How to translate and condense foreign-language articles with Copilot

> **In short:** Paste a foreign-language article into Copilot and ask for a plain English summary, then follow up for the parts you need. Pasted text works most reliably; PDFs and live links vary by account type and plan.

You've probably hit a long article in Spanish, German, Japanese, or Mandarin that you really need to understand — a news piece, a research paper, a product manual, maybe a competitor's announcement from another country. With Microsoft's Copilot assistant, you can paste the text in and walk away with a clear English summary plus translations of the parts that actually matter to you. This guide walks through the whole workflow in five short steps.

## Before you start
- A free Microsoft account (any email works — signing up takes about a minute).
- A modern web browser, or the Copilot app on your phone (free on iOS and Android).
- The foreign-language text ready to paste — copied from a webpage you've already opened, or pulled from a document.
- Roughly 10 minutes for a typical article; longer if it's a dense PDF.

## Step 1 — Open Copilot in a fresh chat
Go to **copilot.microsoft.com** in your browser, or open the Copilot app on your phone. The screen loads to a clean chat window with a message box near the bottom. Starting a fresh conversation matters here: an old chat with earlier topics in it can confuse Copilot and dilute the answer you want. If you don't see a clean empty input area, look for a **"New chat"** or a **"+"** button near the top of the screen. If you're on a Windows 11 computer, Copilot may also live in your taskbar — a small colorful icon.

💬 Example: nothing to type yet — just have the empty chat window open and ready.

You'll know it worked when the message box is empty and waiting for input, with no earlier conversation visible above it.

## Step 2 — Paste the foreign-language text into the chat
Click in the message box and paste the article text. To paste on most computers, press **Ctrl+V** (Windows) or **Cmd+V** (Mac). On a phone, long-press the message box and tap **Paste**. The text appears in the box before you send anything — this is your chance to check that the whole thing came through cleanly. If the article is very long (more than a few thousand words), paste it in sections: Copilot handles chunks better than a single wall of text, and you're less likely to hit a hidden size limit. If your screen shows a red warning or the box refuses the paste, trim the text first and keep only the parts you actually need translated.

💬 Example: just paste the article text directly into the box, no instructions yet — you'll add the ask in the next step.

You'll know it worked when the full article text shows up in the message box, ready to send.

## Step 3 — Ask for a plain English summary
With the text pasted in, type your instruction and send the message. Tell Copilot three things: what language the text is in, how long you want the summary, and that you want plain English (not formal or technical phrasing). Copilot reads your pasted text plus your instruction together and starts drafting a reply. Within a few seconds, a condensed English summary appears in the chat. If the first response feels too dense or uses unfamiliar terms, just ask for a simpler version in a follow-up — Copilot remembers the conversation and will rewrite it.

💬 Example: "This is in German. Please give me a 5-bullet summary in plain English, no jargon, written for a general reader."

You'll know it worked when you see a short, clear English summary that captures the main points of the original article.

## Step 4 — Drill into the parts that matter most
Now you can ask follow-up questions about the specific sections you actually care about. Either quote the exact paragraph from the original you want translated in full, or describe the section by topic. Copilot will translate just that piece, in context, instead of trying to translate the whole article again. This is where the tool really earns its keep: instead of wading through the entire piece, you get the parts you actually need in proper English, with surrounding context preserved. If the translation sounds awkward or stiff, ask for a more natural phrasing — "Can you rephrase that in everyday English?" works well.

💬 Example: "Translate the paragraph about the new tax rules in full, in everyday English. Keep any proper names, dates, and numbers exactly as they are."

You'll know it worked when you get a clean English version of just the section you asked about, with the meaning preserved.

## Step 5 — Copy your summary out for safekeeping
Once you're happy with the summary and the section translations, copy the parts you want to keep. Click and drag to select the English text in Copilot's reply, then copy it the usual way (**Ctrl+C / Cmd+C**, or long-press on a phone), and paste it into your notes app, email, or document. The conversation in Copilot stays available the next time you open it, but having a local copy means you can read it offline, search it later, or share it with someone else. One honest note: Copilot won't reliably read a PDF or article just from a pasted web link, and file uploads aren't available in every version or plan — for important documents, copying the text out and pasting it in (as in Step 2) is the most dependable approach.

💬 Example: nothing to type — just select the text you want and copy it somewhere you'll find it again.

You'll know it worked when the English summary is saved outside Copilot, in a place you control.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting a URL instead of the text.** Copilot often can't fetch the article, especially if it's behind a paywall or a login. Always copy and paste the actual text from the page.
- **Forgetting to say "in plain English."** Without that hint, Copilot may translate literally and keep stiff, formal phrasing that's hard to read. One extra word in your prompt fixes this.
- **Trusting numbers and proper names without checking.** Translations can mistranslate names of people, companies, places, dates, and specific figures. Always glance back at the original for any fact you'll repeat or rely on.
- **Sending a 10,000-word wall of text.** Paste in chunks, or paste just the section you actually need. Very long single pastes can get cut off without warning.
- **Asking for a translation without saying why.** "Translate this" gives a literal word-for-word version; "summarize this for a presentation" gives you something you can actually use. Tell Copilot the purpose and the output improves a lot.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** When you spot an interesting article from abroad — a recipe, a travel guide, a local news story — you can get the gist in under a minute without learning the language.
- **For your business or work:** You can scan foreign-language reports, competitor coverage, or industry news from other countries in a fraction of the time, and pull out the specific quotes, numbers, or rules you need to act on.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with a short article you can also read in the original — that way you can see how well Copilot's summary matches the real meaning, and you'll quickly learn what phrasing gets you the best results.

## Try it now
Find one short article online in a language you don't speak — a French recipe, a German product review, a Japanese travel guide, anything that catches your eye. Copy the first paragraph, paste it into Copilot, and send this exact prompt: *"Summarize this in three plain-English bullet points written for a general reader."* You'll see the whole workflow in action in under two minutes.
